projects.name: HICSS-56 Bayesian Networks
projects.description:
During my internship at Sandia National Labs, I first-authored a research paper under the supervision of Matthew Hoffman and Nathanael Brown within the Mathematical Analysis and Decision Science organization. This paper discusses novel methods in feature selection, random forest MDI discretization, and structural learning for Bayesian network (BN) training and development in the context of cybersecurity attack detection. My research was then published and presented at the 2023 Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences. The abstract and link to download the publication can be found here.

As part of the research, I constructed a Scikit-learn compatible Java to Python extension library that streamlined BN and dynamic BN training and testing pipelines, with applications and use across multiple labs at Sandia.

projects.name: Bayesian Networks for Cybersecurity Attack Detection
projects.description:
This report presents a research-focused project on Bayesian network methods for cybersecurity attack detection. It outlines the development of feature selection, random forest MDI discretization, and structural learning techniques used to improve model interpretability and performance in a security context.

I implemented a Scikit-learn compatible Java-to-Python extension library to streamline Bayesian network and dynamic Bayesian network training and testing workflows, making the methodology easier to apply across multiple research and analysis pipelines.

Read the full report (PDF)

projects.name: Applause Meter
projects.description:
The Applause Meter is a real-time audio monitoring project designed to detect and quantify audience enthusiasm. It uses signal processing and threshold-based analysis to interpret clapping patterns and convert them into a measurable response metric.

This project focused on practical electronics and embedded sensing, with an emphasis on reading environmental sound data and separating meaningful applause from background noise. It is a strong example of applied signal processing in a human-interaction context.
